overview.title: 📖 Overview: Vows of Weight, Height, and a Limb's Worth
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 19a–19b
overview.hebrewSource: הָאוֹמֵר: ״מְשַׁקְּלִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן מִשְׁקָלוֹ, אִם כֶּסֶף כֶּסֶף, וְאִם זָהָב זָהָב
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having closed the chapter of Hesseg Yad (means-tested valuations), the daf opens a new mishna about people who vow to donate their own weight or height to the Temple treasury rather than a fixed Torah valuation. The Gemara works out what material fulfills a weight-vow, tells of a wealthy woman who paid her daughter's weight in gold, and debates how to measure a forearm's weight and a person's height when no simple scale applies. Four related dilemmas are left unresolved. The daf closes with a new mishna on vowing the assessment (damim) of one's forearm — a stringency of vows of assessment over Torah valuations — and the Gemara's attempt to pin down how such an assessment is even calculated.

slides.title: ⚖️ 'My Weight Is Incumbent Upon Me'
slides.subtitle: The mishna's base rule, and how the Gemara expands what counts as payment
rows: If he specified silver or gold, he pays in that
The mishna's 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold' teaches that only a specified metal binds him
If unspecified, any commodity weighed locally suffices
He may 'exempt himself' with whatever merchants in his area sell by weight
Pitch counts, even if some merchants there measure it by volume
Enough that some local merchants weigh it
Onions count, even though sellers throw in two or three extra after weighing
The custom of a small bonus does not cancel its status as a weighed commodity

callout.label: The mother of Yirmatya:
callout.text: She vowed 'my daughter's weight is incumbent upon me' with no metal specified, yet paid in gold. The Gemara resolves this: the mishna is incomplete and really teaches that a distinguished, wealthy person must pay according to their honor even without specifying — and she was such a person.

slides.title: 💧 How Do You Weigh a Forearm?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda's barrel of water against Rabbi Yosei's objection

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: Fill a barrel with water, plunge the arm in up to the elbow, note the water line. Then weigh donkey flesh, bones and sinews and add them until the barrel refills to that line — that weight is what he owes.

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: But how can you match flesh to flesh, bone to bone, sinew to sinew by mere displacement? Volume and weight are not the same thing!

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: One estimates the proportions as best one can.

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: If you're only estimating anyway, skip the barrel — just estimate the arm's weight directly!

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: We still do whatever is possible to be more precise — even an imperfect physical measure beats a pure guess.

callout.label: Scriptural allusion:
callout.text: Though there's no formal proof that donkey flesh weighs like human flesh, R' Yehuda's method is supported by Ezekiel 23:20: 'whose flesh is as the flesh of donkeys.'

slides.title: 📏 My Height vs. My Full Height
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda's ruling, built on Rabbi Akiva's principle that no word is extra

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'My height is incumbent upon me' — Rav Yehuda: give a thick, unbending rod (שַׁרְבִיט שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִכְפָּף) equal to his height
2️⃣ 'My full height is incumbent upon me' — a thin, bendable rod is also acceptable, so long as it equals his height
3️⃣ A baraita objects: both phrasings require the thick, unbending rod — so why does Rav Yehuda distinguish?

4️⃣ Resolution: Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva (Bava Batra 64a, on selling a house 'with its depth and height'), who reads extra words as adding something — so the extra word 'full' must add the option of a thin rod

callout.label: Left unresolved:
callout.text: The Gemara raises but cannot answer (teiku) what one owes for vowing one's stature, width, sitting-height, thickness, or girth.

slides.title: 🖐️ How Far Does 'Hand' or 'Leg' Reach?
slides.subtitle: The Tosefta's water-barrel measure sparks a wider question about the word's scope

nodes.content: ❓ Tosefta: for a forearm-weight vow, immerse the arm 'up to the elbow' (הָאַצִּיל). But for hand-washing in the Temple, 'hands' means only up to the wrist!
💡 Resolution: Torah language (מִקְדָּשׁ) fixes 'hand' at the wrist; but for vows we follow ordinary human speech, where 'hand' reaches the elbow

columns.label: Tefillin
columns.content: 'Your hand' (Ex. 13:9) = the bicep, per the school of Menashe — yet another scope

columns.label: Ḥalitza
columns.content: 'From upon his foot' includes up to the knee — Rav Pappa: the ankle bone is not a separate section

nodes.content: ✅ Each context has its own rule: vows follow colloquial usage; the Temple's wrist-line is a received halakha; tefillin and ḥalitza follow their own verses

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The same Hebrew word (yad, regel) can mean different physical boundaries depending on whether the Torah is speaking about vows, ritual washing, tefillin, or ḥalitza.

slides.title: 🧑‍⚖️ New Mishna: 'The Assessment of My Forearm'
slides.subtitle: A stringency of vows of assessment (damim) over Torah valuations (arakhin) — and two ways to calculate it

boxes.title: Rava's Approach
items: Use the same method as assessing damages (nizakin)
Picture the person as a slave sold in the market: value before the injury minus value after
Abaye objects: that method fits someone who has lost a hand and depreciated — this vower's hand is intact and healthy

boxes.title: Abaye's Refinement
items: Compare the price of a slave who can work with two hands to one who works with only one
Not a slave missing a hand — rather one whose bill of sale reserves his first owner's claim on one hand
This isolates the pure value of 'the use of a forearm' without conflating it with an injury discount

callout.label: Why the mishna is stringent:
callout.text: For Torah valuations (arakhin) there is no valuation of a lone limb at all — 'the valuation of my forearm' says nothing. But for a vow of assessment (damim), the court values it directly, which is why the mishna calls this 'more stringent with regard to vows than with regard to valuations.'

summary.principle: A vow to donate one's own weight, height, or a limb's assessment is fulfilled according to ordinary human usage and honest estimation — not by a fixed Torah scale — and such vows can be more stringent than formal valuations, which apply only to a whole person.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ 'My weight' → pay in the specified metal, or any commodity locally sold by weight
👑 Mother of Yirmatya paid gold unprompted → mishna implies distinguished people pay 'per their honor'

columns.content: 💧 Forearm weight: R' Yehuda's water-barrel estimate vs. R' Yosei's direct estimate
📏 Height: thick rod by default; 'full height' permits a thin rod (R' Akiva's extra-word principle)

flowSteps.content: 🖐️ 'Hand'/'leg' scope shifts by context: vows follow colloquial speech; Temple washing, tefillin, ḥalitza each have their own line
🎓 Key Principle: a vow of assessment (damim) values a single limb directly, comparing a whole person's worth to a diminished one — something arakhin cannot do at all

quiz.q: According to the mishna, if one vows 'my weight is incumbent upon me' without specifying silver or gold, what determines what he must pay?
o: He is entirely exempt
He must always pay in gold
He may pay in any commodity that merchants in his locale sell by weight
He must pay in silver by default
quiz.e: The Gemara infers from the mishna's 'if silver, silver; if gold, gold' that only a specified metal binds him — otherwise any locally-weighed commodity (even pitch or onions, per Raḥava and Rav Pappa) suffices.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile the incident of the mother of Yirmatya, who paid her daughter's weight in gold despite not specifying a metal in her vow?
o: She had actually specified gold and the mishna omitted it
The mishna is incomplete: a distinguished, wealthy person must pay according to their honor even without specifying
Gold is always the default when nothing is specified
The incident does not really concern a weight-vow
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that the mishna is missing text and really teaches that a person of stature pays 'according to their honor' — she was wealthy, so gold was expected of her even absent a specification.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Yosei's objection to Rabbi Yehuda's water-barrel method for weighing a forearm-vow?
o: Water cannot be used in a barrel for Temple purposes
Displacement measures volume, not weight, so donkey flesh, bones, and sinews cannot be precisely matched to the person's own flesh, bones, and sinews
Donkey flesh is forbidden to bring near the Temple treasury
The vow can only be fulfilled with money, never with physical measurement
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei points out that the barrel measures volume by displacement, while weight is a different quantity, so matching donkey parts to human parts by volume cannot be precise — better to estimate the arm's weight directly.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Yehuda rule that 'my full height' (as opposed to just 'my height') permits donating a thin, bendable rod?
o: Because 'full' always means the largest possible payment
Following Rabbi Akiva's principle that extra, unnecessary language in a statement comes to add something new
Because thin rods are cheaper and therefore the default
Because the word 'full' cancels the vow entirely
quiz.e: The Gemara traces this to Rabbi Akiva's method (seen regarding a house sale 'with its depth and height') of deriving added meaning from superfluous wording — since 'full' need not have been said, it adds the leniency of a thin rod.

quiz.q: Why is the new mishna's law of 'the assessment (damim) of my forearm' described as more stringent than a Torah valuation (erekh) of a forearm?
o: Because damim vows are punished with lashes while arakhin vows are not
Because arakhin values a whole person only, so 'the valuation of my forearm' means nothing, whereas a damim vow lets the court directly assess the forearm's worth
Because damim vows apply only to gold, never silver
Because arakhin vows can never be paid by heirs
quiz.e: Torah valuations (arakhin) are fixed sums that apply only to an entire person, so a vow on a single limb 'says nothing' under arakhin. A vow of assessment (damim), by contrast, lets the court appraise that limb's value directly — hence the stringency.
